Cairngorms: Scotland's Mighty Mountain National Park

The Cairngorms National Park is the UK's largest national park, covering over 1,748 square miles of the central Scottish Highlands. It contains four of Scotland's five highest mountains, the largest remnants of the ancient Caledonian pine forest, and sub-arctic plateaux that support wildlife found nowhere else in Britain. For motorcyclists, the Cairngorms deliver Britain's highest public road, world-class whisky distilleries, and some of the finest touring roads in Scotland.

The Highest Road in Britain

The A93 over the Cairnwell Pass reaches 665 metres at its summit, making it the highest public road in Britain. Running from Blairgowrie to Braemar, this A-road climbs through increasingly dramatic scenery before crossing the pass at the Glenshee Ski Centre. The descent into Braemar is spectacular, with views of the surrounding Munros. The road surface is generally excellent, though winter closures are common from November to March.

Speyside and Whisky

The northeastern section of the park is dominated by Speyside — the heart of Scotch whisky production. The Malt Whisky Trail connects distilleries including Glenfiddich, Macallan, Glenlivet, and Cardhu. Even if whisky isn't your thing (you are riding, after all), the distillery buildings and their riverside settings are beautiful. Plan a rest day and book a tasting tour — Glenfiddich and Macallan both offer excellent visitor experiences.

  • Glenfiddich, Dufftown — Scotland's most visited distillery, excellent free tour
  • The Macallan, Craigellachie — Stunning modern visitor centre, premium tours
  • The Glenlivet — Remote setting, excellent tour explaining whisky heritage
  • Cardhu — The only distillery pioneered by a woman, fascinating history

Ancient Forests and Wildlife

The Cairngorms harbour remnants of the ancient Caledonian pine forest — the forest that once covered Scotland after the last ice age. Rothiemurchus Forest near Aviemore is the most accessible section. Red squirrels are common, ospreys nest at Loch Garten, and if you're very lucky you might spot a Scottish wildcat or golden eagle. Reindeer were reintroduced to the Cairngorm plateau in 1952 and can be visited on guided walks.

The Cairngorms are Scotland at its most elemental. The mountains here are bigger, the forests older, and the wildlife wilder than anywhere else in Britain. Come for the roads, stay for everything else.

Key Destinations

Aviemore is the main gateway town — it has gear shops, restaurants, and accommodation ranging from hostels to luxury hotels. Braemar, on the eastern side, is a quieter base near Balmoral Castle. Grantown-on-Spey is an elegant Victorian town on the edge of Speyside. Kingussie and Newtonmore are pleasant villages with access to the Laggan Road — a superb motorcycle route through the central Highlands.

Best Riding Roads

  • A93 Cairnwell Pass — Britain's highest road, Blairgowrie to Braemar
  • A939 Tomintoul to Grantown — Known as the Lecht road, often the first in Britain to close for snow
  • A86 Laggan Road — Sweeping Highland road from Kingussie to Spean Bridge
  • B970 Feshiebridge to Kincraig — Quiet road through Inshriach Forest with mountain views
  • A9 through the Drumochter Pass — High-speed dual carriageway at 462 metres altitude

Practical Information

The Cairngorms are accessed via the A9 from Perth (1.5 hours) or Inverness (45 minutes). From Edinburgh, allow 2.5 hours to Aviemore. Fuel is available in Aviemore, Grantown-on-Spey, Braemar, and Kingussie, but there's nothing on the high mountain passes. The weather can be extreme — the Cairngorm summit has recorded wind speeds exceeding 170mph and snow can fall in any month. Stick to valley roads in poor weather. Best months: May to September, though autumn colours in October are breathtaking. Midges can be ferocious from June to August in sheltered areas — carry repellent. faq.q: What is the highest public road in Britain?
faq.a: The A93 over the Cairnwell Pass reaches 665 metres at its summit, making it the highest public road in Britain. Running from Blairgowrie to Braemar, it climbs through increasingly dramatic scenery before crossing the pass at the Glenshee Ski Centre. The surface is generally excellent, but winter closures are common from November to March.

faq.q: Can I visit whisky distilleries while riding the Cairngorms?
faq.a: Speyside, in the park's northeast, is the heart of Scotch whisky production, with the Malt Whisky Trail linking Glenfiddich, Macallan, Glenlivet and Cardhu. Since you are riding, plan a rest day and book a tasting tour rather than sampling between stages. Glenfiddich and Macallan both offer excellent visitor experiences.

faq.q: Where should I base myself in the Cairngorms?
faq.a: Aviemore is the main gateway town, with gear shops, restaurants and accommodation from hostels to luxury hotels. Braemar on the eastern side is a quieter base near Balmoral Castle, Grantown-on-Spey is an elegant Victorian town on the edge of Speyside, and Kingussie and Newtonmore give access to the superb Laggan Road.

faq.q: How changeable is the Cairngorms weather?
faq.a: The weather can be extreme. The Cairngorm summit has recorded wind speeds exceeding 170mph and snow can fall in any month. Stick to valley roads in poor weather rather than the high passes. The best months are May to September, though the autumn colours in October are breathtaking. Fuel is available in the main towns but not on the high passes.

faq.q: How do I get to the Cairngorms?
faq.a: The Cairngorms are accessed via the A9 from Perth in about 1.5 hours or from Inverness in 45 minutes. From Edinburgh, allow 2.5 hours to Aviemore. Fuel is available in Aviemore, Grantown-on-Spey, Braemar and Kingussie, but there is nothing on the high mountain passes, so fill up before crossing them.
